problem_statement: The paper frames machine learning as a task that is used in fields including financial analysis, and focuses on the core operation of classifying high-dimensional vectors into clusters or labels. It presents this as the basic mathematical routine behind supervised and unsupervised machine learning.
problem_statement_quotes: Machine learning, a branch of artiﬁcial intelligence, learns from previous experience to optimize performance, which is ubiquitous in various ﬁelds such as computer sciences, ﬁnancial analysis, robotics, and bioinformatics.

The core mathematical task for both supervised and unsupervised machine learning algorithm is evaluating the distance and inner products between the high-dimensional vectors to analyze the similarity between vectors
The aim is to classify new examples based on these training sets.
classical_baseline: The paper treats classical machine learning as the baseline, where distances and inner products between high-dimensional vectors are computed on classical computers to classify data into clusters or nearest neighbors. It also refers to the latest supercomputers as the classical resource that would perform this work.
classical_baseline_quotes: The core mathematical task for both supervised and unsupervised machine learning algorithm is evaluating the distance and inner products between the high-dimensional vectors to analyze the similarity between vectors, which requires a time proportional to the size of the vectors on classical computers.
The new sample is assigned to the cluster to which the distance is smaller.
With rapidly growing data size in the modern world, such a task could pose a challenge even for the latest supercomputers.
classical_difficulty: The paper says the classical difficulty is that evaluating distances and inner products scales with vector size on classical computers, so rapidly growing data can make the task intractable or challenging even for supercomputers. It also notes that the quantum algorithm can achieve a time O(log(MN)) for assigning vectors to clusters, highlighting the classical scaling issue by contrast.
